text.p: Copper prices were steady while nickel headed higher on the London Metals Exchange on Thursday. Wheat futures closed mostly lower, pulled down by a drop in soybean and corn futures
METALS - Copper prices shied away from revisting the level above $2,270 hit overnight during Thursday LME trading, although widening spread premiums kept the market steady, traders said.
Borrowers were in evidence throughout the session, keeping the dates between now and the February prime all tight and likely to be in excess of $20.
Cash/Feb was at $127 backwardation, while Feb/threes was some $90. This lifted the cash/threes premium to $230 by the close, against Wednesday's $207.

LME stocks on Friday are expected to register another increase, although traders doubt whether there will be a significant rise, as some metal will be removed from warehouses. A rise of between 5,000 and 10,000 tonnes is being talked about.

Three months prices, meanwhile settled for consolidation having threatened to break higher yesterday. Shortcovering kept values above $2,250, and last business was at $2,257, up $17 a tonne from Wednesday's kerb.

Despite the signals being sent from copper, aluminium again lacked the impetus to drive higher - specifically above the $1,625 level. Producer sales are expected between $1,640 and $1,650, and this is inhibiting buying interest.
Last business was at $1,622.50, a $9.50 loss from the overnight close. On the downside, a test of $1,600/10 cannot be ruled out.
Nickel raced higher during the late kerb, breaking back above $7,800, and momentarily hitting a new 7-1/2 month high of $7,890 before last trade at $7,880, up $70 from Wednesday.

The late upturn was also seen in zinc where the market bounced away from the mid-$1,170 level, although prices did not reach Wednesday's two-year peaks near $1,190. Last business was at $1,187, up $3.
Market sentiment is firmly pointed to the upside at present, with the investment fund interest seen recently adding to a constructive fundamental picture of falling stocks.
The lead market was, by comparison, somewhat subdued, and encountered difficulty near $680. Prices closed at $679, a $2 loss.
The tin market clawed its way higher, but the move was unconvincing and business was fairly slow. Three months finished at $5,890, up $30 from the previous close.
Alloy prices held barely steady in thin trading, with the market restrained by primary's tardiness. Last business was at $1,530, down $5.

GOLD - New York precious metals futures closed mostly lower Thursday, except for palladium which saw a fresh four month high, but volumes were only moderate. "It's going to be tough for gold to recover much, as producers are waiting to hedge on any bounce, but there's been a distinct lack of interest in doing very much since gold fell below $350 recently," Mitsui & Co USA bullion dealer Greg Drury said. COMEX April gold ended down $1.30 an ounce at $345.10, after seeing a new contract low at $344.00. Total estimated COMEX gold futures volume was 30,000 lots.

WHEAT - CBOT wheat futures closed mostly lower, pulled down by a drop in soybean and corn futures, traders said. Corn and beans were hit by bearishly-construed crop production estimates in the Clinton budget for 1998. The fiscal 1998 budget proposed for the Agriculture Department pegged 1997 U.S. wheat production at 2.345 billion bushels of wheat. Early this week, the U.S. Feed Grains Council said 1997 U.S. wheat production would total 2.449 billion bushels. Wheat closed four cents a bushel lower to 1/2 cent higher, with March down 3-1/2 at $3.58.

NYMEX OIL - NYMEX crude hovered around sharply lower levels Thursday afternoon, poised to take out its session low after an early technical sell-off sent oil prices into a tailspin. "The floor seems to think its going to fall through the low. After two o'clock (1400 EST), traders will return from lunch, and we will see what happens," said a New York dealer. March crude was 67 cents lower at $23.24 a barrel after setting a session low this morning of $23.15.
